description.narrative: Reporting is an important management tool which is used to inform relevant government officials and other stakeholders about the results being achieved by individual projects and the programme as a whole. For project partners, it is compulsory to use the prescribed Orange Knowledge annual report format in order to report on project achievements. The annual report also provides valuable data on the financial situation of the project. Based on an analysis of the project performance in relation to the project output(s) and expected outcome(s), a revision of the project work plan may be suggested by the project partners. The consequences of a possible revision on the project work plan and budget must be made clear in the annual report. Nuffic monitors outputs and outcomes and not activities . Therefore, the main focus of the annual report must be on the achievement of the project’s output(s) and planned outcome(s). The information provided in the annual reports of the projects is used by Nuffic to monitor the progress of the project and to inform the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and other stakeholders about the output(s) and outcome(s) being achieved by individual projects and the Orange Knowledge programme as a whole. Please note that if project progress is in accordance with the original planning, reporting requirements are minimal. Only in case of deviations from the planning, more elaboration is demanded. In the grant award letter, the dates for submission of the annual reports are mentioned. In case of a three-year project, between 5-7 reports are obligatory. The first report (0) is a very short report which focuses on specific conditions and/or recommendations in the grant. There is no need to report on progress in achieving outputs and outcomes, which is done in the first annual report. As annex to the report 0, the consortium agreements between the partners should be submitted. The final report must reflect on the entire project period.

actual.value:
The training project consisted of a training preparation phase and three workshops and aimed at 3 main outputs. The final workshop took place in Bujumbura on October 6th, 2022. The outputs are presented below, as well as a summary of the extent to which they have been reached:
​
**1. ISABU staff have acquired relevant skills and are confirmed in their co-ordinating role of practical policy change implementation.**
​
ISABU staff, and staff of other organizations present in the training, have acquired relevant skills in analyzing farmers' grass-roots (potato) export support needs, to analyse sectoral needs in regulatory deregulation or adaptation, to identify the agro-economic opportunities in export, to undertake export-facilitating/enabling activities, to fast-track regulatory approval procedures (e.g. in case of admitting seeds for new exportable potato varieties), to solve export preparation and implementation bottlenecks (e.g. in generating collaboration and advocacy with their colleagues in other countries, in case of 'non-tariff' barriers to agro-export to these countries), as well as to set up and maintain the problem-oriented internal and external communication and consultation processes that are required for it.
​
Most striking conclusion of training participants is that the attainment and application of most of the above skills not really requires the acquisition of extra knowledge, but rather better communication and collaboration. Between the relevant government agencies, while acting on a jointly agreed and enacted focus on the real grass-roots production and exporting needs of the rural agro-producers.
​
Further, the second component did not materialize, and for obvious reasons. In the TMT workshop where this issue was discussed, participants agreed that ISABU can _**initiate**_ policy change, for instance to undertake research, presenting the results and stipulating the ensuing policy change recommendations, but it is not its prerogative to _**co-ordinate**_ policy implementation, let alone the change of existing policies. that is the authority of the policy sections of the Ministry of Agriculture.
​
**2. A practical and operational policy re-orientation agenda is established with relevant partners**
​
In the discussion about various examples of successes of and setbacks in government agencies facilitating and supporting Burundian farmers' agro-exports, training participants concluded that further improvements do not really require policy reorientation, but rather improved procedures for communication and collaboration between the government agencies involved.
​
Various instances were identified where this communication and collaboration was hampered by e.g.:
_- politicization_ (e.g. a minister promises something non-feasible to politicians, does not take 'not possible' for an answer, his staff are passing the hot cup on to their colleagues in research organizations, again not taking 'not possible' for answer, and in the end everyone stops communicating), or
_-resource -control orientation_ (e.g. research agencies developing income streams by taking on delivery of agricultural services that have been developed by their own research, or agencies not committed to collaboration unless they can manage funding flows and budgets. In either way access to funds inevitably grows more important than co-ordinated success).
​
So within the training the participants agreed on improved procedures to identify bottlenecks and opportunities in the export sector and to involve relevant government agencies in a transparent and traceable way in the prioritization of the activities of support to export by Burundian farmers, client (farmers) relation management, reporting and assessment of the results of the interventions. This e.g. in the field of fast-tracking the admission of seeds for export varieties, testing of new potato varieties, more effective phytosanitary quality assurance support to farmers (advise, inspection, labelling of traceable lots), as well as in the field of relations management with colleague organizations in neighboring countries regarding application of export regulations and , if needed, phytosanitary counter-expertise activity.
​
A case in point is the issue of mechanization of seed potato farming in Burundi. Markets in neighboring countries have a high demand for clean and affordable seed potatoes (as does the internal market in Burundi,, by the way..), but seed potato production training in Burundi has been dominated by (NL-financed) NGOs invariably aiming at training groups of poorly resourced farmers who keep on struggling with diseases in their seed potatoes. If the export markets and the domestic demand are to be effectively serviced, the TMT participants from different government services concluded jointly, mechanization of seed potato production becomes inevitable, allowing for improved phytosanitary quality assurance during the seed potato multiplication stages and for higher tonnages of seed tubers produced and marketed in more uniform batches.
In the final training workshop the participants developed a joint 'road map' for mechanization of seed potato production that stipulates the objectives, roles, tasks and input timing of the relevant government agencies in a process to prepare and implement a pilot project fore seed potato mechanization. One of the first steps, taken shortly after the TMT training has closed and hence being a follow-up activity of it, is a joint visit of senior ISABU and Ministry of Agriculture staff to a mechanized seed potato farm in Uganda, that could practically guide and inspire the development of a similar pilot enterprise in Burundi.
During that mission, practical arrangements will be made for practical internship of Burundian agronomic staff of relevant departments, as well an agreement and a framework developed for the fundraising and investment in a public-private learning farm in mechanized seed potato production Burundi . To make this project a success, various government entities will need to co-ordinate and collaborate, gaining along the road valuable knowledge and operational experience for tackling opportunities and bottlenecks in other agro-export value chains in future.
​
**3. A government services-initiated and maintained change process is initiated that practically aligns with and reinforces the private seed sector development activities supported by Netherlands embassy-supported projects, especially the Private Seed Sector Development project.**
As described above under the achievements of output no. 2., a government services-initiated change process is initiated, and in its objectives it aligns with the private seed sector development activities as supported by the Netherlands embassy. However, with the Private Seed Sector Development project (PSSD) little meaningful and practical interaction took place in the course of 2022 as the latter came to the end of its project period, and had decommissioned almost all of its personnel by the time the final concluding workshop the tailor-made training course was prepared and implemented.
​
